card.title: Dulong and Petit Method of Determining Expansivity of Liquid

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Dulong and Petit's method measures a liquid's **real cubical expansivity** by cancelling the vessel effect. The apparent expansion in any vessel obeys $\gamma_a = \gamma_r - \gamma_g$; using the same liquid in two vessels of coefficients γ₁ and γ₂ gives $\gamma_2 - \gamma_1 = \gamma_{a1} - \gamma_{a2}$ — a relation independent of the liquid.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - γ_a = γ_r − γ_g - γ₂ − γ₁ = γ_{a1} − γ_{a2} - γ_g = 3α (vessel material)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Liquid Columns in Communication: Two limbs must contain same liquid connected at bottom — pressure equality at bottom.  ·  Different Temperatures: One limb maintained at reference (e.g., 0°C), other at known higher temperature.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The difference of the apparent expansivities in two vessels equals the difference of the cubical expansivities of the vessels."

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **The trick is cancellation:** the liquid's expansion difference between two vessels equals the vessels' expansion difference — no direct measurement of tiny expansions needed.  ·  **Apparent = real − vessel:** keep the signs straight.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Weighing an Invisible Expansion Liquids expand far too little to measure directly by eye. Dulong and Petit's genius was to *cancel* the vessel's contribution: the same liquid in two different vessels shows level rises that differ by exactly the liquid's true expansion. The apparatus turns an apparent effect into an absolute measurement.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Principle A liquid's **apparent** expansion in a vessel = real expansion − vessel's expansion: $$\gamma_a = \gamma_r - \gamma_g$$ In two vessels of cubical coefficients $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ (same liquid, same ΔT): $$\gamma_{a1} = \gamma_r - \gamma_1, \qquad \gamma_{a2} = \gamma_r - \gamma_2$$ Subtracting: $$\boxed{\gamma_2 - \gamma_1 = \gamma_{a1} - \gamma_{a2}}$$ — the…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Write γ_a = γ_r − γ_g for both vessels, then subtract."

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Measure differences, not absolutes:** Dulong–Petit sidesteps the impossible direct measurement of a liquid's true expansion.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: γ_a = γ_r − γ_g; two vessels ⇒ γ₂ − γ₁ = γ_{a1} − γ_{a2}.  ·  Apparatus: two bulbs (different materials) + U-tube, heated uniformly.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Dulong and Petit also gave the law of constant atomic heat capacity (1818) — unrelated but bearing their name.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### Deep dive: apparent vs real expansivity A liquid has no shape of its own, so its expansion is always measured *relative to a container*.
